item.title: A Whole New Side: The Duality Symmetries of Hitomezashi
item.description: arXiv:2608.27542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hitomezashi is a particular style of sashiko stitching characterized by crossing lines of stitches. Certain hitomezashi designs can be encoded with two binary strings and have been the subject of a wide-array of mathematical research. Dubbed generalized hitomezashi patterns (GHPs) by Sen & Martinez, these designs are reversible and can be 'self-dual.' We investigate the possible 'dual-' or 'flip-symmetries' in GHPs; the inclusion of these symmetries is equivalent to considering two-colour symmetry groups. Following the work of Sen & Martinez, who found the wallpaper symmetry groups that are compatible with GHPs, this paper investigates the possible two-colour symmetries compatible with GHPs. We prove that there are four possible rosette two-colour symmetry types, completely describe the properties on binary strings that create these symmetries, and prove that exactly 17 of the 46 two-colour wallpaper groups are compatible with GHPs.
item.dc:creator: Megan A. Martinez

item.title: On the Egyptian knotted rope
item.description: arXiv:2608.28072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Egyptian knotted rope has been historically considered a measuring/geometric tool. A naive change in the way the rope is held to tighten it turns the rope into a primitive calculating tool --- a sort of primitive abacus. The arithmetic skills of the knotted rope have a double interest. From an historical point of view, they fit perfectly with some of the basic ancient Egyptian computing techniques. From an educational point of view, they enhance the potential interest of the knotted rope as a useful manipulative in mathematical education.
item.dc:creator: Rub\'en Vigara

item.title: The Mathematician Leads: Building a Research Profile in the Age of Frontier AI
item.description: arXiv:2608.28369v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I propose that mathematicians who use AI in research maintain a research profile: a record of what the system has learned about working with them, where those lessons came from, and whether they remain useful. I describe how such a profile grew out of my own mathematical work, through corrections, failed approaches, and repeated attempts to keep difficult ideas from drifting toward easier ones. The profile is not a portrait of the mathematician and does not replace mathematical judgment. It belongs under the mathematician's control and must remain open to revision. I invite others to develop profiles of their own and report what they learn.
item.dc:creator: Helmut H. W. Hofer
